prompt: why does white glue actually stick paper together
reply:
White glue is a crowd of tiny plastic-like particles floating in water 🧪. The water carries them into the gaps between paper fibres, then evaporates, and the particles fuse into one film hardened around the fibres. So the grip is mechanical, more like roots than a weld. Glue two scraps, dry them fully, then pull, and it should tear beside the join.

prompt: why is corrugated cardboard so strong for how light it is
reply:
Look at a cut edge: two flat sheets with a wave glued between them 📦. The wave holds the faces apart, and bending stiffness climbs fast as the faces separate, which is the same reason a steel I-beam is mostly hole. On edge, along the waves, it carries a real load. Push across the waves and it crushes.

prompt: why does cardboard go weak the moment it gets wet
reply:
Paper is a mat of tangled cellulose fibres, held to each other by hydrogen bonds, weak alone but powerful in their millions 💧. Water molecules slip in and take those bonds over, so the fibres let go and slide past each other. The glue holding the corrugated layers softens too, and the waves flatten. Dry it out and it never gets all its strength back.

prompt: why does my air dry clay shrink and warp as it dries
reply:
Air dry clay is solid particles floating in water, so every drop that leaves lets the particles pull closer and the piece has to get smaller 🏺. The surface dries first and tries to shrink around a wet, full-size core, and something has to give. Thick lumps are the worst offenders, which is why potters hollow them out. Slow it down with a loose bag, even walls and no direct sun.
